questions.question: A dense transformer applies its feed-forward network to every token. What does a sparse MoE change?
options: A position embedding selects one encoder layer
A router selects a subset of experts per token
A tokenizer maps each word to several subwords
A decoder generates more than one token at once
questions.explanation: A sparse MoE replaces the dense FFN with experts plus a router, which selects k experts for each token. A position embedding does not choose computation paths; the router’s top-k decision creates conditional sparsity.

questions.question: With E = 256 experts and top-k = 8, what percentage of routed experts is active for one token?
options: 0.39% of routed experts
3.125% of routed experts
100% of routed experts
0.03125% of routed experts
questions.explanation: Eight of 256 routed experts gives 8/256 = 0.03125 of the experts, or 3.125%. The 0.39% option is the percentage for one expert out of 256, not the selected group of eight.

questions.question: In auxiliary-loss-free balancing, how does the per-expert bias affect routing?
options: It changes gate weights, not top-k selection
It replaces raw router scores in the main objective
It updates expert parameters through a new loss
It changes top-k selection, not gate weights
questions.explanation: The balancing bias is added to router scores to alter top-k selection, but gates are computed from the original scores. Changing gates rather than selection would change mixture weights without correcting which experts receive traffic.

questions.question: What is the role of a shared expert in DeepSeek-V3’s split?
options: It stores the key and value cache for all tokens
It replaces the decoder’s cross-attention layer
Every token passes through it for common knowledge
Only tokens with the highest router score pass through it
questions.explanation: A shared expert processes every token and captures common knowledge, while top-k routed experts specialize. Restricting it to highest-scoring tokens would make it routed rather than shared.

questions.question: A 671B MoE uses only 37B active parameters per token. What deployment constraint still matters?
options: The active parameter count is the total VRAM requirement
Only the selected experts need to be stored anywhere
All expert weights must fit across the serving GPUs
The router removes network communication between GPUs
questions.explanation: The 37B active figure describes computation per token, not the model’s full weight storage. All experts must reside across the serving GPUs even when a particular token uses only a few of them.

questions.question: A team wants frontier quality at lower per-token compute and has expert-parallel GPU capacity. Which architecture is the lesson’s fit?
options: A tiny encoder with a fixed classifier head
A dense transformer with every FFN active
A mixture of experts with top-k routing
A recurrent model with one shared hidden state
questions.explanation: MoE fits this constraint because top-k routing activates only a subset of expert FFNs per token while retaining a large total parameter pool. A dense transformer activates every FFN, so its per-token compute does not get that sparsity benefit.
